title: Problem Set 2: Population & Marketplaces
text:
Q1. Combine the world shape world with population (point) data and with ports & airports data.
Q2. Create maps & histograms regarding country-level population and average distances to nearest port/airport, segmented by continent.




 Goal : Combine the world shape world with:

Population (point) data (do not use rasters!)
Ports, airports, etc.





The data comes from two different sources, the spData library (which contains the “world” shapefile) and Natural Earth (Data Source). Specifically, from Natural Earth we download:

Populated Places dataset
Airports dataset
Ports dataset




First of all, we load the datasets.


Show the code
sf.world <- world
st_crs(sf.world)$input


[1] "EPSG:4326"




Show the code
sf.cities <- st_read('Data/ne_10m_populated_places/ne_10m_populated_places.shp',quiet = T)
st_crs(sf.cities)$input


[1] "WGS 84"




Show the code
sf.airports <- st_read('Data/ne_10m_airports/ne_10m_airports.shp', quiet = TRUE)
st_crs(sf.airports)$input


[1] "WGS 84"




Show the code
sf.ports <- st_read('Data/ne_10m_ports/ne_10m_ports.shp', quiet = TRUE)
st_crs(sf.ports)$input


[1] "WGS 84"


All datasets utilise the WGS84 coordinate reference system, hence no projection conversion is required.
For cleanliness, we filter the datasets to keep only the variables essential for this project.


Show the code
sf.world <- sf.world %>%
  select(name_long, continent, area_km2, geom) %>% # we are dropping pop because we will later compute it using the cities dataset
  rename(name = name_long) %>%
  # Adding type column
  mutate(type = "COUNTRY") %>%
  relocate(type, .before = everything())

sf.cities <- sf.cities %>%
  select(NAME, geometry, POP_MAX) %>% # keeping population to be able to rank the cities
  rename(name = NAME, geom = geometry, pop = POP_MAX) %>%
  # Adding type column
  mutate(type = "CITY") %>%
  relocate(type, .before = everything())
  
sf.airports <- sf.airports %>%
  select(name, geometry, scalerank) %>% # keeping scalerank to be able to rank the airports
  rename(geom = geometry) %>%
  # Adding type column
  mutate(type = "AIRPORT") %>%
  relocate(type, .before = everything())

sf.ports <- sf.ports %>%
  select(name, geometry, scalerank) %>%
  rename(geom = geometry) %>%
  # Adding type column
  mutate(type = "PORT") %>%
  relocate(type, .before = everything())






We need to identify the country and continent for every city, airport, and port. To do so, we will create an auxiliary dataset with only the country, continent, and geom columns of the world dataset, and then merge them based on their spatial information.


Show the code
# Adding country column also to the world dataset
sf.world <- sf.world %>%
  mutate(country = name)

# Creating the auxiliary dataset
sf.world.aux <- sf.world %>%
  select(country, continent, geom)

# Adding the country and continent columns to the datasets
sf.cities <- st_join(sf.cities, sf.world.aux, join = st_intersects)
mean(is.na(sf.cities$country)) * 100 # computing percentage of NAs in the country column over the total observations


[1] 6.442386


Show the code
sf.cities <- sf.cities %>%
  arrange(country)

sf.airports <- st_join(sf.airports, sf.world.aux, join = st_intersects)
mean(is.na(sf.airports$country)) * 100


[1] 11.64614


Show the code
sf.airports <- sf.airports %>%
  arrange(country)

sf.ports <- st_join(sf.ports, sf.world.aux, join = st_intersects)
mean(is.na(sf.ports$country)) * 100


[1] 28.58464


Show the code
sf.ports <- sf.ports %>%
  arrange(country)


Our operation generated a lot of NA’s, especially in the airport and port datasets. This probably happens because some coastal locations are mapped slightly outside the country borders. Therefore, when using st_intersect, they don’t intersect with any country in the world dataset, generating NA’s.
To fix this, we will undo the last step and try again using a 10km buffer.


Show the code
# Reverting to the original datasets
sf.airports <- sf.airports %>%
  select(- country, - continent)

sf.ports <- sf.ports %>%
  select(- country, - continent)

# Adding the country and continent columns to the datasets
sf.airports <- st_join(sf.airports, sf.world.aux, join = st_is_within_distance, dist = 10000)
sf.airports <- sf.airports %>%
  arrange(country)
mean(is.na(sf.airports$country)) * 100


[1] 7.359307


Show the code
sf.ports <- st_join(sf.ports, sf.world.aux, join = st_is_within_distance, dist = 10000)
sf.ports <- sf.ports %>%
  arrange(country)
mean(is.na(sf.ports$country)) * 100


[1] 10.05435


This buffer fixed a lot of the missing values. However, this operation may not be totally accurate. For example, since some small islands are missing from our world map, a port may be assigned to the wrong country if it is withing 10km of its borders. Also, ports on islands that are further than 10 km away from the coastline are still not detected.


Show the code
# Aggregating population by country
country_pop <- sf.cities %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>% # dropping geometry since we don't need it for this 
  group_by(country) %>%
  # Summing pop column of cities in the same country
  summarise(pop = sum(pop, na.rm = TRUE))

# Joining the calculated population to the world dataset
sf.world <- sf.world %>%
  left_join(country_pop, by = "country") %>%
# Moving geom to the last column for tidyness 
  relocate(geom, .after = everything())


Now we will merge the datasets into one single dataset.


Show the code
sf.data <- bind_rows(sf.world, sf.cities, sf.airports, sf.ports)

# Rearrange by type
sf.data <- sf.data %>%
  arrange(type)






Produce:

Map of total population by country
Histogram of country population distribution by continent
Histogram of (country-level) average distances between locations and ports or airports by continent. If there are too many locations and/or airports, filter the top 20 of them.

For ease of use and code tidiness, we will use the unmerged datasets.


To visualize population distribution, we will combine the world dataset with the cities dataset. First, we will plot the countries, using a color gradient to show their total population. Then, we will overlay the cities, grouping them into seven size categories to highlight population concentration.



OECD classifies urban areas as:

large metropolitan areas if they have a population of 1.5 million or more;
metropolitan areas if their population is between 500 000 and 1.5 * million;
medium-size urban areas if their population is between 200 000 and 500 000; and,
small urban areas if their population is between 50 000 and 200 000.

We will also add two more categories:

Megacities (population greater than 10M)
Towns (population from 5k to 50k)
Villages (population lower than 5k)

Our categories are:

Very low (< 5k population)
Low (5k to 50k population)
Medium-Low (50k to 200k population)
Medium (200k to 500k population)
Medium-High (500k to 1.5M population)
High (1.5M to 10M population)
Very high (> 10M population)



Show the code
sf.cities <- sf.cities %>%
  mutate(pop_cat = cut( # creating categorical column for population
    pop,
    # Binning the population data
    breaks = c(- Inf, 5000, 50000, 200000, 500000, 
               1500000, 10000000, Inf),
    # Adding labels
    labels = c("Very Low", "Low", "Medium-Low", "Medium", "Medium-High",
               "High", "Very high"),
    right = FALSE
  ))

st_drop_geometry(sf.cities) %>%
  count(pop_cat) # See if some categories do not contain many cities 


      pop_cat    n
1    Very Low  854
2         Low 2273
3  Medium-Low 2188
4      Medium 1020
5 Medium-High  702
6        High  286
7   Very high   19


The distribution of the cities looks okay, with very few cities in the “Very High” category (as expected). The NA’s are two very small cities present in the dataset which have negative population, which won’t affect our final analysis.



To keep the map readable, we will limit the number of cities shown for each country based on its size. Larger countries will show more cities, while smaller countries will show fewer


Show the code
# Auxiliary dataset
country_data <- sf.world %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>% 
  select(country, area_km2) # Keep only what we need

# Filtering cities based on Country Size
sf.cities.plot <- sf.cities %>%
  # Join the area data to the cities
  left_join(country_data, by = "country") %>%
  
  # Define the "City Limit" rules
  mutate(
    max_cities = case_when(
      area_km2 < 20000   ~ 1,
      area_km2 < 100000  ~ 3,
      area_km2 < 350000  ~ 6, 
      area_km2 < 1000000 ~ 10,
      area_km2 < 5000000 ~ 15,
      TRUE               ~ 25
    )
  ) %>%
  
  # Applying the filter
  group_by(country) %>%
  arrange(desc(pop)) %>%                # Sort largest to smallest
  filter(row_number() <= max_cities) %>% # Keep only the allowed amount
  ungroup()


Finally, we generate our plot.


Show the plotting code
# Plotting
ggplot() +
  
  # World map
  geom_sf(data = sf.world, aes(fill = pop), color = "white", size = 0.05) +
  scale_fill_gradient( # gradient based on the country's population
    low = "#deebf7",
    high = "#08306b",
    name = "Country Pop", 
    trans = "log", # logarithmic scale so that the gradient is not completely skewed towards China and India
    labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale()), # formatting the labels to make them more readable
    guide = guide_colorbar(
      title.position = "left", 
      title.hjust = 0.5,
      barwidth = 15, 
      barheight = 0.4,
      order = 1 
    )
  ) +
  
  guides(
    # Hiding shape and size legends
    shape = "none",
    size  = "none",
    
    # Keepig the color and putting title on Left
    color = guide_legend(
      title.position = "left", 
      title.vjust = 0.5, 
      nrow = 1, 
      order = 2)) + 

  # Cleaning
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + 
  theme_void() + 
  theme(
    
    # Legend
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.box = "vertical",
    legend.margin = margin(t = 10, b = 10, l = 10, r = 10),
    legend.box.margin = margin(t = -10, b = -10, l = 0, r = 0),
    
    # Image margins
    plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10, b = 0, l = 10, unit = "pt"),
    
    # Text styles
    legend.title = element_text(size = 8, face = "bold", color = "grey20"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 6, color = "grey30"),
    legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm")
  )

Show the code
# Filter the data set to have only population and joint everything by country

sf.data_pop <- sf.data %>% 
  filter(type == 'CITY') %>% 
  group_by(country) %>% 
  summarize(population = sum(pop))

ggplot(sf.data_pop, aes(x = population)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, colour = '#08306b', fill = '#08519c') +
  labs(x = 'Population',
       y = 'Count', 
       title = 'World Population Distribution, by Country') +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = c("0", "100M", "200M", "300M"),
    breaks = c(0, 100000000, 200000000, 300000000)
  ) +
  theme_minimal()+ 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5))









Show the code
extremes <- sf.data_pop %>% 
  filter(population > 50000000)


Because the histogram with the current non-modified data is skewed to the left due to some extreme values from China, USA, India etc, we decided to compute the histogram applying a log scale to the population.


Show the code
# Compute the log of the population variable

sf.data_pop <- sf.data_pop %>%  
  mutate(log_pop = log(population))

ggplot(sf.data_pop, aes(x = log_pop)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, colour = '#08306b', fill = '#08519c') +
  labs(x = 'Log Population',
       y = 'Count', 
       title = 'World Population Distribution, by Country (log scale)') +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5))












To have a more detailed information on the population density we decided to compute the same log histograms for each of the continents.


Show the code
sf.data_pop <- sf.data_pop %>% 
  left_join(sf.world.aux %>% 
              st_drop_geometry() %>% 
              select(country, continent), 
            by = 'country')

ggplot(sf.data_pop, aes(x = log_pop)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, aes(fill = continent), colour = 'black') +
  facet_wrap(~ continent, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = 'Distribution of Country Population by Continent',
    x = 'Population',
    y = 'Number of Countries'
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust=0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray40", hjust=0.5),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90", colour = NA),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )











Show the code
ggplot(sf.data_pop, aes(x = population)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, aes(fill = continent), colour = 'black') +
  facet_wrap(~ continent, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = 'Distribution of Country Population by Continent',
    x = 'Population',
    y = 'Number of Countries'
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust=0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray40", hjust=0.5),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90", colour = NA),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )









By plotting the population distributions by continent without the log scale we clearly see exactly the same as before, there are some outliers in each continent that make the distribution skewed to the left.





Show the code
# Use data set sf.data
# Compute distance between cities and ports and airports by country
# Combine ports and airports
library(units)
sf.transport <- sf.data %>% filter(type %in% c('PORT', 'AIRPORT'))
sf.locations <- sf.data %>% filter(type == 'CITY')

# Calculate distance matrix to all transport hubs
distance_matrix <- st_distance(sf.locations$geom, sf.transport$geom)

# Get minimum distance for each city
sf.locations <- sf.locations %>%
  mutate(
    distance_to_nearest = apply(distance_matrix, 1, min), 
    distance_km = as.numeric(distance_to_nearest) / 1000   # Convert to km
  )

# Calculate country-level averages
country_distances <- sf.locations %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(country, continent) %>%
  summarize(avg_distance_km = mean(distance_km, na.rm = TRUE), 
            .groups = 'drop') %>%
  filter(!is.na(continent))




Show the plotting code
# plot
ggplot(country_distances, aes(x = avg_distance_km)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, aes(fill = continent), colour = 'black', alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ continent, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = 'Distribution of Country Average Distances to Nearest Transport Hub',
    subtitle = 'Average distance from cities to nearest airport or port by continent',
    x = 'Average Distance',
    y = 'Number of Countries'
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust=0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray40", hjust=0.5),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90", colour = NA),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )









With the average distance in km for each continent, we cannot extract much information when we compare the distribution across continents. We take the log again.


Show the code
ggplot(country_distances, aes(x = log(avg_distance_km))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, aes(fill = continent), colour = 'black', alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ continent, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = 'Log Distribution of Country Average Distances to Nearest Transport Hub',
    subtitle = 'Log Average distance from cities to nearest airport or port by continent',
    x = 'Log Average Distance',
    y = 'Number of Countries'
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust=0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray40", hjust=0.5),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90", colour = NA),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )









From the plots above using the log transformation, several insights can be highlighted. Africa shows higher average distances between cities and transport hubs compared to Europe, which may reflect less developed infrastructure, greater geographic dispersion of cities, or the continent’s larger land area. Europe and North America present similar distributions, with most countries clustered at lower average distances, suggesting well-developed and accessible transport networks.
South America shows less variability in average distances than Africa but centers around similar mean values, indicating moderate transport accessibility with less inter-country variation. Oceania, with fewer countries, exhibits high variability in average distances, likely due to the diverse geographic characteristics of island nations versus continental Australia. Asia displays the widest distribution, with many countries showing high average distances, potentially reflecting the continent’s vast size, varied development levels, and geographic diversity.

Produce:

Map of total population by country
Histogram of country population distribution by continent
Histogram of (country-level) average distances between locations and ports or airports by continent. If there are too many locations and/or airports, filter the top 20 of them.

For ease of use and code tidiness, we will use the unmerged datasets.


To visualize population distribution, we will combine the world dataset with the cities dataset. First, we will plot the countries, using a color gradient to show their total population. Then, we will overlay the cities, grouping them into seven size categories to highlight population concentration.



OECD classifies urban areas as:

large metropolitan areas if they have a population of 1.5 million or more;
metropolitan areas if their population is between 500 000 and 1.5 * million;
medium-size urban areas if their population is between 200 000 and 500 000; and,
small urban areas if their population is between 50 000 and 200 000.

We will also add two more categories:

Megacities (population greater than 10M)
Towns (population from 5k to 50k)
Villages (population lower than 5k)

Our categories are:

Very low (< 5k population)
Low (5k to 50k population)
Medium-Low (50k to 200k population)
Medium (200k to 500k population)
Medium-High (500k to 1.5M population)
High (1.5M to 10M population)
Very high (> 10M population)



Show the code
sf.cities <- sf.cities %>%
  mutate(pop_cat = cut( # creating categorical column for population
    pop,
    # Binning the population data
    breaks = c(- Inf, 5000, 50000, 200000, 500000, 
               1500000, 10000000, Inf),
    # Adding labels
    labels = c("Very Low", "Low", "Medium-Low", "Medium", "Medium-High",
               "High", "Very high"),
    right = FALSE

The distribution of the cities looks okay, with very few cities in the “Very High” category (as expected). The NA’s are two very small cities present in the dataset which have negative population, which won’t affect our final analysis.



To keep the map readable, we will limit the number of cities shown for each country based on its size. Larger countries will show more cities, while smaller countries will show fewer

  st_drop_geometry() %>% 
  select(country, area_km2) # Keep only what we need

# Filtering cities based on Country Size

  # Join the area data to the cities

  # Define the "City Limit" rules
  mutate(
    max_cities = case_when(
      area_km2 < 20000   ~ 1,
      area_km2 < 100000  ~ 3,
      area_km2 < 350000  ~ 6, 
      area_km2 < 1000000 ~ 10,
      area_km2 < 5000000 ~ 15,
      TRUE               ~ 25
    )
  ) %>%
  
  # Applying the filter
  group_by(country) %>%
  arrange(desc(pop)) %>%                # Sort largest to smallest
  filter(row_number() <= max_cities) %>% # Keep only the allowed amount
  ungroup()

# Use data set sf.data
# Compute distance between cities and ports and airports by country
# Combine ports and airports
library(units)

sf.locations <- sf.data %>% filter(type == 'CITY')

# Calculate distance matrix to all transport hubs

# Get minimum distance for each city
sf.locations <- sf.locations %>%
  mutate(
    distance_to_nearest = apply(distance_matrix, 1, min), 
    distance_km = as.numeric(distance_to_nearest) / 1000   # Convert to km
  )

# Calculate country-level averages
country_distances <- sf.locations %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(country, continent) %>%
  summarize(avg_distance_km = mean(distance_km, na.rm = TRUE), 
            .groups = 'drop') %>%
  filter(!is.na(continent))




Show the plotting code
# plot
ggplot(country_distances, aes(x = avg_distance_km)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, aes(fill = continent), colour = 'black', alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ continent, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = 'Distribution of Country Average Distances to Nearest Transport Hub',
    subtitle = 'Average distance from cities to nearest airport or port by continent',
    x = 'Average Distance',
    y = 'Number of Countries'
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust=0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray40", hjust=0.5),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90", colour = NA),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )









With the average distance in km for each continent, we cannot extract much information when we compare the distribution across continents. We take the log again.


Show the code
ggplot(country_distances, aes(x = log(avg_distance_km))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, aes(fill = continent), colour = 'black', alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ continent, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = 'Log Distribution of Country Average Distances to Nearest Transport Hub',
    subtitle = 'Log Average distance from cities to nearest airport or port by continent',
    x = 'Log Average Distance',
    y = 'Number of Countries'
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust=0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray40", hjust=0.5),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90", colour = NA),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )









From the plots above using the log transformation, several insights can be highlighted. Africa shows higher average distances between cities and transport hubs compared to Europe, which may reflect less developed infrastructure, greater geographic dispersion of cities, or the continent’s larger land area. Europe and North America present similar distributions, with most countries clustered at lower average distances, suggesting well-developed and accessible transport networks.
South America shows less variability in average distances than Africa but centers around similar mean values, indicating moderate transport accessibility with less inter-country variation. Oceania, with fewer countries, exhibits high variability in average distances, likely due to the diverse geographic characteristics of island nations versus continental Australia. Asia displays the widest distribution, with many countries showing high average distances, potentially reflecting the continent’s vast size, varied development levels, and geographic diversity.

Goals

Q2. Calculate minimum distance of each market to the (i) coast, (ii) nearest road, and (iii) nearest airport
Q3. Produce 3 scatter plots relating average prices with the minimum distances

Reference Paper:
Porteous, O., 2019. High trade costs and their consequences: An estimated dynamic model of African agricultural storage and trade. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 11(4), pp.327-66.
Direct link: Paper


Packages used:


Show the code
rm(list=ls())
library(sf)
library(tidyverse)
library(spData)
library(osmdata)
library(readxl)

title: Problem Set 2: Population & Marketplaces
text:
Data and sources
To complete this assignment, we will need data from several sources. First, we will use the spData library, which contains the world shapefile. In addition, we will need datasets for roads, highways, airports, and the coastline, as well as data from the replication paper that features marketplaces across Africa.
Sources:

Airports
Highways and Roads
Coastline
Market Locations and Prices


Loading the Data
First we create a polygon from the world shape file in spData so we can use it to filter through intersections with other datasets


Show the code
africa <- world %>%  filter(continent == "Africa")

africa_poly <- africa %>% 
  summarise(geom = st_union(geom), .groups = "drop")


We load the different shapefiles for the roads, the coastline and the airports:


Show the code
africa_roads_raw<-st_read("Data/groads-v1-africa-shp/gROADS-v1-africa.shp", quiet = TRUE) #Roads data

africa_roads_clean<- africa_roads_raw %>%
  filter(LENGTH_KM >= 20) %>%
  st_crop(africa_poly) %>%              
  st_intersection(africa_poly)  

coastline<-st_read("Data/ne_10m_coastline/ne_10m_coastline.shp", quiet = TRUE)
coastline_africa <- st_intersection(coastline, africa)



airports<-st_read("Data/ne_10m_airports/ne_10m_airports.shp", quiet = TRUE)
airports_africa  <- st_intersection(airports, africa)


For the Africa roads layer, we apply two filters. First, we keep only roads with LENGTH_KM >= 20 so that smaller roads are not considered. We choose this for a couple of reasons; first, because computationally it is very expensive to compute intersections and distances for over 500k+ road observations, so reducing the size of this dataset is beneficial to the efficiency of our task execution; second, because this is a much more relevant analysis of the data – we care more about the distance a market has to a more important, well-connected road than it does to some random neighborhood or back road that may only spans one kilometer and connects to very few homes.
Second, we clip the roads to the Africa polygon (africa_poly) derived from the world dataset, because the roads shapefile also includes features from the Middle East and the southern part of Europe. We use st_intersection() for an exact spatial clip to Africa and we apply the same concept to the coastline data and the airports data.

title: Problem Set 2: Population & Marketplaces
text:
Q2.2: Calculate Min Distances
We can combine what we have obtained before with the roads data to obtain the following plot:


Show the code
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = africa, fill = "grey95", color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = africa_roads_clean, aes(color = "Roads"), 
          linewidth = 0.3, key_glyph = draw_key_path) +
  geom_sf(data = mkt_pts, aes(color = "Markets"), size = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Legend",
    values = c(
      "Markets" = "red",
      "Roads"   = "grey30"
    ),
    breaks = c("Markets", "Roads")
  ) +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(
      override.aes = list(
        linewidth = c(0, 1),
        shape     = c(16, NA),
        size      = c(3, 0)
      )
    )
  ) +
  labs(title = "Roads and Markets in Africa") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    legend.margin = margin(6, 6, 6, 6),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5)
  )









And combine the previous plot with the the coast and airport data:


Show the code
ggplot() +
  # Africa background
  geom_sf(data = africa, fill = "grey95", color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4) +

  # Roads
  geom_sf(
    data = africa_roads_clean,
    aes(color = "Roads"),
    linewidth = 0.3,
    alpha = 0.6,
    key_glyph = draw_key_path
  ) +

  # Coastline
  geom_sf(
    data = coastline_africa,
    aes(color = "Coastline"),
    linewidth = 0.4,
    key_glyph = draw_key_path
  ) +

  # Airports
  geom_sf(
    data = airports_africa,
    aes(color = "Airports"),
    size = 1.2,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +

  # Market points
  geom_sf(
    data = mkt_pts,
    aes(color = "Markets"),
    size = 1.5
  ) +
  
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Legend",
    values = c(
      "Roads"     = "grey30",
      "Coastline" = "purple",
      "Airports"  = "#1f78b4",
      "Markets"   = "red"
    ),
    breaks = c("Markets", "Airports", "Roads", "Coastline")
  ) +
  
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(
      override.aes = list(
        linewidth = c(0, 0, 1, 1),
        shape     = c(16, 16, NA, NA),
        size      = c(3, 3, 0, 0),
        alpha     = c(1, 1, 1, 1)
      )
    )
  ) +
  labs(title = "Infrastructure and Markets in Africa") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    legend.margin = margin(6, 6, 6, 6),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5)
  )










Computing the distances
To compute the minimum distance:


Show the code
# Nearest feature index for each market
idx_coast   <- st_nearest_feature(mkt_pts, coastline_africa)
idx_road    <- st_nearest_feature(mkt_pts, africa_roads_clean)
idx_airport <- st_nearest_feature(mkt_pts, airports_africa)


We want the minimum distance for each market individually and we want to compute it efficiently and correctly, without building a huge distance matrix or mixing markets together, st_nearest_feature() tells us which feature is the closest one to each market.
Then we compute the distance only to that feature:


Show the code
# Minimum distance (meters) to the nearest feature (by element)
d_coast_m <- st_distance(mkt_pts, coastline_africa[idx_coast, ], by_element = TRUE)
d_road_m  <- st_distance(mkt_pts, africa_roads_clean[idx_road, ],      by_element = TRUE)
d_air_m   <- st_distance(mkt_pts, airports_africa[idx_airport,], by_element = TRUE)

# Attach to the markets table (convert to numeric km)
mkt_pts <- mkt_pts %>%
  mutate(
    dist_coast_km   = as.numeric(d_coast_m) / 1000,
    dist_road_km    = as.numeric(d_road_m)  / 1000,
    dist_airport_km = as.numeric(d_air_m)   / 1000
  )


For each market location, we compute the minimum Euclidean distance to the three types of spatial infrastructure: the coastline, the road network, and the nearest airport. This is done using the st_distance() function.
Before computing distances, each market is matched to its nearest feature of the relevant type (coast, road, or airport). Using these matches, st_distance() is applied with the option by_element = TRUE, which ensures that distances are calculated pairwise, which makes that each market is compared only to its own nearest feature rather than to all features in the dataset. As a result, the output is a vector of minimum distances, one value per market, expressed in meters, which correspond to the coordinate reference system of the spatial data.
The resulting distance vectors are then added to the markets dataset as new variables. Distances are converted from meters to kilometers by dividing by 1,000 and stored in three different variables: distance to the coast, distance to the nearest road, and distance to the nearest airport.
We can check the mean distances for each of the three variables:


Show the code
summary(mkt_pts$dist_coast_km)


     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max. 
   0.1478  178.1537  530.0659  571.5270  925.7852 1736.1293 


Show the code
summary(mkt_pts$dist_road_km)


     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max. 
7.255e-03 9.458e-01 3.044e+00 1.165e+01 1.069e+01 1.238e+02 


Show the code
summary(mkt_pts$dist_airport_km)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   1.11   24.30  201.73  229.19  338.24  915.61 


It can be seen that each variable has very different interpretation as its values vary deeply:

Distance to coast: On average, markets are located about 572km from the coastline, indicating that many markets are substantially inland.
Distance to roads: Markets are, on average, about 11.7km away from the nearest major road, suggesting relatively good road accessibility (We have to consider the filter of minimum 20km length applied in the beginning for the roads for this interpretation, which means that if the filter was not applied we could expect a lower distance on average).
Distance to airports: The average distance to the nearest airport is approximately 229km, implying limited proximity to air transport infrastructure for most markets.

We could also inspect an specific market row:


Show the code
i <- 5  # pick a market row to inspect

title: Class 03: Geometry Operations
text:
Main reference for these notes is Lovelace, R., Nowosad, J. and Muenchow, J., 2019. Geocomputation with R. Chapman and Hall/CRC. https://r.geocompx.org/geometry-operations
This chapter, quote: “…focuses on manipulating the geographic elements of spatial objects.” This includes:

Simplification: reducing memory size by reducing geometries
Centroids: calculating the center of mass of a geometry object
Buffers: generate buffer zones surrounding a geometry
Casting: transform between geometry types
Clipping: restricting geometry space b/w two objects
Distances: calculating distance b/w one or two geometry objects
Transformations: shifting, scaling, and rotations

style=“color:blue”>Geometry Operations are manipulations of vector data that manipulates its geometry.
Here are the main libraries we will use for these notes:

library(sf)           # simple-features library
library(terra)        # spatial data analysis
library(tidyverse)    # tidyverse: data manipulation, ggplot
library(spData)       # gives us example spatial datasets
library(spDataLarge)  # gives us example large spatial datasets
library(patchwork)    # put ggplots side-by-side
library(rmapshaper)   # for ms_simplify()
library(smoothr)      # for smooth()

title: Class 03: Geometry Operations
text:
Motivation: Coastline Paradox
Let’s say you’re trying to measure the length of coastline of a nation, say Iceland. Further, imagine that we are measuring the coastline using a 500km ruler. The resulting measurement will be quite inaccurate, much lower than the true coastline length since we cannot account for small edges and turns.
Then, we use a 100km ruler to measure the coastline and obtain a new measurement, which is still inaccurate, but our measured coastline value has now increased as our margin of error decreases as we are able to account for more details of the curves around the coastline.
Now imagine this measurement process iteratively:
500km -> 100km -> 10km -> 1km -> …. -> tracing around every pebble and grain of sand -> … -> tracing around every Planck length of matter.
What do we think happens to the value we obtain for the coastline?
Essentially, the length of our coastline approaches infinity as our our measurement device records smaller and smaller values. This result is obviously impossible, since the length of a coastline has to be a finite value. Thus, we arrive at the Coastline Paradox, first noted by Lewis Fry Richardson in the 1920s.






500km Ruler Measurement: 3000km







100km Ruler Measurement: 4000km







1km Ruler Measurement: 4500km





Put in more formal terms, where \(n\) is the length of our measurement device, and the function \(f(n) = \frac{1}{n}\) gives us the basic inverse relationship between coastline length and length of measurement device:
\[
\lim_{n \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{n} = \infty
\]






Inverse Relationship between Length of Coastline & Length of Measurement Device





The reason for this phenomena is fractals: if we start very zoomed out, everything looks quite “smooth”, and we see the outline of bays and peninsulas. As we zoom in further, we see that each bay as its own inlet; even further, that each inlet has rocky shorelines; further, each individual rock has crevices; sand grains have irregular edges; and so forth.












Fractals











Theoretically, our measurement devices are capable of approaching measuring lengths \(\rightarrow 0\). However, in reality this is not possible nor feasible; as some point, the measurements would flatten enough where even smaller measurements would not affect the length of the coastline at some significance level. Further, it not physically possible to create measuring devices of such a microscopic scale.
What does this paradox have to do with our geospatial data?
When computing spatial geometries, these types of geometries & their associated calculations can take up a lot of memory in exchange for very precise maps. Thus, we might want to take a extremely precise map, measured with very ‘small’ measuring sticks, and scale it back to a more inaccurate map, in exchange for more memory storage.
Indeed, we can see from Euclidean geometry that the length of a curve can be approximated using straight lines that connecting various points on the curve. Although not the exact arc length of our curve, this approximation helps us to build ‘shortcuts’ where we sacrifice super precise representations of our maps/geometries in exchange for way more computational power. Of course, this trade-off must be balanced; we still need to accurately represent our maps to an audience and not risk losing too many data points from our simplification process.



Approximation of a Curve by Summing Straight Lines


This leads us into our first unary operator (works on a single geometry in isolation): Simplification.
Found in the sf package, our function of choice here is sf_simplify().

title: Class 03: Geometry Operations
text:
Seine Example
For example, we can see below how the sf_simplify() function reduces the complexity of the map of the rivers in France:

# st_simplify with 2000m 'measuring stick'
seine_simple <- st_simplify(seine, dTolerance = 2000) # 2000m



Show plotting code
# here we use the sf library to access the geom df `seine`

# original data
p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=seine, color = "black", linewidth=0.65) +
  labs(title = "Original Data") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )

# simplified data
p2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=seine_simple, color = "black", linewidth=0.65) +
  labs(title = "st_simplify()") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )

p1 + p2









As we can see, after using st_simplify our graph has much less complexity, with fewer vertices. We can verify that it is computationally friendlier as a result:

# memory usage of og data
object.size(seine)

18096 bytes

# memory usage of simplified data
object.size(seine_simple)

9112 bytes


Note the makeup of the st_simplify function is very simple:
st_simplify(x = sfg, sfc, or sf object, preserveTopology = logical, dTolerance = numeric)
Where:

preserveTopology: logical, default is TRUE; asks whether to avoid invalid geometries (self-intersections, border crossings, etc). TRUE is much safer, more conservative; FALSE simplifies as much as possible, but allows for weird occurances in the geometry.
dTolerance: numeric; controls for how simplified we want our graph. Lower value corresponds to preserving the original geometry; higher values simplify the graphs more and more. Can think of this as the ‘length’ of our new measuring stick we want to use.

title: Class 03: Geometry Operations
text:
Transforming
For example, to transform (shift) a map of New Zealand, we can simply add values to adjust the x and y-coordinates:

# extract geom column from nz sf object
nz.sfc <- st_geometry(nz)

# shift every geom value y-value by 100000m (1000km)
nz_shift_y <- nz.sfc + c(0,100000)
st_crs(nz_shift_y) <- st_crs(nz)
nz_shift_y.sf <- st_set_geometry(nz, nz_shift_y) # assign new geoms back to og sf

# shift every geom value x-value by 50000m (500km)
nz_shift_x <- nz.sfc + c(50000,0)
st_crs(nz_shift_x) <- st_crs(nz) # set our trans geom to match our og CRS
nz_shift_x.sf <- st_set_geometry(nz, nz_shift_x)



Show plotting code
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=nz, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill = "darkgray") +
  geom_sf(data=nz_shift_x.sf, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="skyblue",alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data=nz_shift_y.sf, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="salmon",alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "TRANSFORMATION") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),

title: Class 03: Geometry Operations
text:
Scaling
Scaling our maps involves enlarging our shrinking objects by a factor. We can adjust these scales globally, to affect every point in our geometry; for example,

# shrink every geom value by 0.5
nz_global_center <- st_centroid(st_union(nz.sfc)) # GLOBAL center
nz_global_scale <- (nz.sfc - nz_global_center) * 0.5 + nz_global_center
st_crs(nz_global_scale) <- st_crs(nz)
nz_global_scale.sfc <- st_set_geometry(nz, nz_global_scale)

Note that to get the global centroid, we need to take union of all our geometries using the st_union() function, after which we can apply to it st_centroid.


Show plotting code
p1<-ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=nz, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="gray") +
  geom_sf(data=nz_global_scale.sfc, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="skyblue",alpha = 0.5) +
  #geom_sf(data=nz_scale_inc.sfc, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="salmon",alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "GLOBAL SCALING") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )


Or we can adjust these scales locally, treating geometries independently and requires points around which geometries are going to be scales (centroids, for example):

# extract geom column from nz sf object
nz.sfc <- st_geometry(nz)

# shrink every geom value y-value by 0.5
nz_centroid.sfc <- st_centroid(nz.sfc) # LOCAL centers
nz_scale <- (nz.sfc - nz_centroid.sfc) * 0.5 + nz_centroid.sfc
st_crs(nz_scale) <- st_crs(nz) 
nz_scale.sfc <- st_set_geometry(nz, nz_scale)



Show plotting code
p2<-ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=nz, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill = "darkgray") +
  geom_sf(data=nz_scale.sfc, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="skyblue",alpha = 0.5) +
  #geom_sf(data=nz_scale_inc.sfc, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="salmon",alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "LOCAL SCALING") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )

p1+p2

title: Class 03: Geometry Operations
text:
Rotation
Finally, we can rotate our graphs using a rotation matrix of the following form:
\[
R =
\begin{bmatrix}
  cos\theta & -sin\theta \\
  sin\theta & cos\theta
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Which rotates points in a clockwise direction. We can define a rotation function as the following:

rotation = function(degrees){
  r = degrees * pi / 180 #degrees to radians
  matrix(c(cos(r), sin(r), -sin(r), cos(r)), nrow=2, ncol=2)
}

We can implement this to rotate around selected points, such as centroids:

# extract geom column from nz sf object
nz.sfc <- st_geometry(nz)

# global rotation
nz_global_center <- st_centroid(st_union(nz.sfc)) # GLOBAL center
nz_rotate_global <- (nz.sfc - nz_global_center) * rotation(90) + nz_global_center
st_crs(nz_rotate_global) <- st_crs(nz)
nz_rotate_global.sfc <- st_set_geometry(nz, nz_rotate_global)

# local rotations
nz_centroid.sfc <- st_centroid(nz.sfc) # centers we will shrink around locally (each region)
nz_rotate_local <- (nz.sfc - nz_centroid.sfc) * rotation(90) + nz_centroid.sfc
st_crs(nz_rotate_local) <- st_crs(nz) 
nz_rotate_local.sfc <- st_set_geometry(nz, nz_rotate_local)



Show plotting code
p1 <-ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=nz, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill = "darkgray") +
  geom_sf(data=nz_rotate_global.sfc, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="skyblue",alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "GLOBAL ROTATION") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )

  geom_sf(data=nz, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill = "darkgray") +
  geom_sf(data=nz_rotate_local.sfc, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="salmon",alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "LOCAL ROTATIONS") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),

title: Class 01: Intro to Vector Data & sf Library
text:
Basics
We have three basic geometries for our vector data: points, lines, & polygons
These geometries are stored as arrays: numeric vectors, matrices, & lists

Shapes

1. Points
Simplest form of geometry; typically translate to (LONG, LAT)
A single POINT is declared using the command st_point, by passing in a single numeric vector:

# single point
geom_point <- c(2,4)
single_pt <- st_point(geom_point)
st_as_text(single_pt)

[1] "POINT (2 4)"


whilst a collection of points is known as MULTIPOINT, declared using the command st_multipoint command, which expects a numeric matrix (specifically a 2D array):

# multiple points
geom_multipoints <- rbind(c(2,4), c(1,5), c(0,2), c(1,0))
multipts <- st_multipoint(geom_multipoints)
st_as_text(multipts)

[1] "MULTIPOINT ((2 4), (1 5), (0 2), (1 0))"




2. Lines
Lines are simply a collection of points connected sequentially (meaning the ordering of our points matters!)
A single LINESTRING can be constructed from a 2D numeric array, the same exact way as a MULTIPOINT, only now using the command st_linestring:

# single line
geom_multipoints <- rbind(c(2,4), c(1,5), c(0,2), c(1,0))
single_line <- st_linestring(geom_multipoints)
st_as_text(single_line)

[1] "LINESTRING (2 4, 1 5, 0 2, 1 0)"


We can also construct multiple linestrings, known as MULTILINES using the command st_multilinestring: expects a list of numeric matrices (2D arrays).

# multiple lines
geom_multilines <- list(rbind(c(2,4), c(1,5), c(0,2), c(1,0)),
                        rbind(c(0,0), c(1,1), c(2,2), c(3,3)),
                        rbind(c(1,1), c(1,0), c(1,-1)))
multi_lines <- st_multilinestring(geom_multilines)
st_as_text(multi_lines)

[1] "MULTILINESTRING ((2 4, 1 5, 0 2, 1 0), (0 0, 1 1, 2 2, 3 3), (1 1, 1 0, 1 -1))"




3. Polygons
Finally, we can create shapes by building lines as we did before, but now making sure the first point & last point are the same. Polygons require a list of numeric array(s)
A single POLYGON follows the same logic as MULTILINES, now with the same coordinates for the first and last points. We use now the command st_polygon to build this object:

# single line
geom_singlepoly <- list(rbind(c(2,4), c(1,5), c(0,2), c(1,0), c(2,4)))
single_poly <- st_polygon(geom_singlepoly)
st_as_text(single_poly)

[1] "POLYGON ((2 4, 1 5, 0 2, 1 0, 2 4))"


We can, like before with lines, build & assign multiple POLYGONS to a single object, aptly named a MULTIPOLYGON. The difference for this is that we must input a list of lists; i.e. a list of single polygons, using the command st_multipolygon

# single line
geom_multipoly <- list(list(rbind(c(3,4), c(3,3), c(5,3), c(5,4), c(3,4))), # rectangle
                        list(rbind(c(1,4), c(1,5), c(2,4), c(1,4)))) # right triangle
multi_poly <- st_multipolygon(geom_multipoly)
st_as_text(multi_poly)

[1] "MULTIPOLYGON (((3 4, 3 3, 5 3, 5 4, 3 4)), ((1 4, 1 5, 2 4, 1 4)))"





Simple Features (sf)
SIMPLE FEATURE:

SF COLUMN (GEOMETRY + PROJECTION) +
ATTRIBUTE (DATA FRAME)

title: Class 01: Intro to Vector Data & sf Library
text:
Example 1: spatial geometries


Code
# multipoint (think: long-lat)
multipt_matrix <- rbind(c(3.2, 4), c( 4, 4.6), c(3.8, 4.4),
                           c(3.5, 3.8), c(3.4, 3.6), c(3.9, 4.5))
gm.multipt <- st_multipoint(multipt_matrix)

# linestring (connecting pts; order matters)
linestring_matrix <- rbind(c(0, 3), c(0,4), c(1,5), c(2,5))
gm.linestr <- st_linestring(linestring_matrix)

# polygon (last pt & first pt must match)
angle <- seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = 100)
circle_coords <- cbind(3.5 + 0.5*cos(angle), 0.5 + 0.5*sin(angle))
polygon_matrix <- list(list(rbind(c(0,0), c(1,0), c(3,2), c(2,4), c(1,4), c(0,0))),
                       list(rbind(circle_coords, circle_coords[1,])))
gm.poly <- st_multipolygon(polygon_matrix)

# create these objects into a column: st_sfc
geom <- st_sfc(gm.multipt, gm.linestr, gm.poly)

# our normal (non-geom) dataframe
mock_data <- data.frame(objects = c('multipt', 'linestr', 'polyg'))

# append our geom data to our data_frame, declare it as a sf object
sf_mockdata <- st_sf(mock_data, geometry = geom)

# plot our shapes!
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=sf_mockdata, fill = "lavender") +
  theme_minimal()










Projections
The world is a 3D object: when we try to project this onto a 2D surface (like a map), it is impossible to not have distortion (proven by Gauss, known as the “Theorema Egregium” – reference for a deeper dive into the math).
The basic idea behind the differential geometry is that a (2D) plane has \(K=0\) Gaussian curvature, whilst a (3D) sphere w/ radius ‘R’ has a constant & strictly positive curvature, \(K=\frac{1}{R^2}\). There does not exist a function to perfectly map the plane to the sphere (and vice versa); consequentially, every cartographic projection must contain at least some distortion between distances.



Map Projection Distortion


Thus, we need to pay attention to what sort of projection structure our data has. There exists a plethora of ways to project the globe onto a map; what is important is that these projections are both:

well-defined, and
standardized (agree in their projections)

Otherwise when we try to build our spatial models, we might end up at completely incorrect coordinates. The ‘standard’ (most common) longitude-latitude used is Geodetic CRS: WGS 84; passed as an argument as crs = 'EPSG:4326'. For example:

gm.point <- st_point(c(11.3, 44.4)) # c(longitude,latitude)
gmc.point <- st_sfc(gm.point,
                    crs = 'EPSG:4326')
gmc.point; st_as_text(gmc.point)

Geometry set for 1 feature 
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 11.3 ymin: 44.4 xmax: 11.3 ymax: 44.4
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84


[1] "POINT (11.3 44.4)"


What if we have an array (2D matrix) of multipoints that dont have a projection assigned to them? for example:

df.cities <- data.frame(
  name = c('Bologna', 'London', 'Madrid', 'Paris'),
  temperature = c(31, 21, 29,28),
  language = c('Italian', 'English', 'Spanish', 'French'),
  longitude = c(11.3,-0.1,-3.7,2.3),
  latitude = c(44.4,51.5, 40.4,48.8)
)
# Declare the data frame as an sf object, & declare our 'coords' col as the geometry
sf.cities <- st_as_sf(df.cities,
                      coords = c('longitude', 'latitude'))
sf.cities # Missing CRS!

Simple feature collection with 4 features and 3 fields
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: -3.7 ymin: 40.4 xmax: 11.3 ymax: 51.5
CRS:           NA
     name temperature language          geometry
1 Bologna          31  Italian POINT (11.3 44.4)
2  London          21  English POINT (-0.1 51.5)
3  Madrid          29  Spanish POINT (-3.7 40.4)
4   Paris          28   French  POINT (2.3 48.8)


Notice the output for CRS: NA – it is important to specify and/or standardize!

# Correct version
sf.cities <- st_as_sf(
  df.cities,
  coords = c('longitude', 'latitude'),
  crs = 'EPSG:4326'
  )

sf.cities

title: Class 04: Intro to Raster Data
text:
Loading & Creating
To declare a raster object, we use the command rast() to initialize this object. If we investigate the object further, we can find some useful information:

r <- rast()
r

class       : SpatRaster 
size        : 180, 360, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
resolution  : 1, 1  (x, y)
extent      : -180, 180, -90, 90  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
coord. ref. : lon/lat WGS 84 (CRS84) (OGC:CRS84) 


Note some important features:

resolution: the total span of our ‘window’, divided by the number of grids. by default is \(1\times1\), which means that each grid is exactly \(1^{o} \text{ longitude} \times 1^{o} \text{ latitude}\). A small resolution value means: more cells (pixels), more detail, larger file size, and slower processing (>1 grid per \(1^o\times1^o\) ‘box’.
extent: the ‘window’ our raster object takes. By default, this is a projection of the world map, using by default the WGS84 CRS
size: related to extent & resolution, this is the nrow \(\times\) ncol of our matrix (window). A 1$$1 resolution means that the there is a 1:1 match between the numbers of grids and number of rows & number of columns.


head(values(r)) # 'matrix' treated as a very long vector

     lyr.1
[1,]   NaN
[2,]   NaN
[3,]   NaN
[4,]   NaN
[5,]   NaN
[6,]   NaN

# in r it fits the matrix horizontally

Further investigation reveals that by default, the raster has no values stored. If we tried plotting it, we would return an empty plot; thus, we need to assign values to the object. Note that although our ‘window’ we are attempting to plot is a matrix, R stores this value as a vector that it then transposes and assigns row-by-row (in Python it acts the same, but assigns the values column-by-column, which could cause discrepancies if working between the two softwares).
Note that since our grid is \(180 \times 360\) with \(1 \times 1\) resolution, we have a total of \(64800\) cells.
To assign values, we can simply assign sequential values to the object by assigning each value to its corresponding place in the grid; i.e., since our grid has \(64800\) cells, we assign the value to each cell that corresponds to its position: the \(1\times1\) cell gets assigned a value of \(1\), the \(1\times2\) cell a value of \(2\), and so forth.
Note: we can also manipulate these cell values to get different types of grids; for example, if we to generate a grid of “white noise”, we can randomly & uniformly generate & assign values to the cells.
# sequential assignment of values to cells
values(r) <- 1:ncell(r)
plot(r)

# random assignment of values to cells
r2 <- rast()
values(r2) <- runif(1:ncell(r))
plot(r2)











(a) Sequential Value Assignment











(b) Random Value Assignment







Figure 1: Comparison of Grid Values



We immediately see the concepts come to life: each cell that represents a value can be mapped to a color scheme, which allows us to create powerful and super detailed pictures at scale. Of course, this comes at a cost of very high computational needs, so there is a very large trade-off here between accuracy (resolution) and memory.
We can overlay our vector map objects on the raster grid. For example, we can plot the map of Brazil using our ‘world’ dataset from our spData library.

sf.brazil <- world %>% 
  filter(iso_a2=='BR')

plot(r)
plot(st_geometry(sf.brazil), add=T)








However, we see that although we filtered for Brazil, our grid still is the entire world map projection. Thus, we need to introduce operations to adjust this window size.

title: Class 04: Intro to Raster Data
text:
Cropping
The crop() function works by trying to fit our raster matrix (“r”) into the extent of a vector object (“sf.Brazil”).

r.crop <- crop(r, sf.brazil)
plot(r.crop)








Note that our grid axes have now changed. We can now replot the ‘Brazil’ sf object overlayed on this cropped window:

plot(r.crop)
plot(st_geometry(sf.brazil), add=T)








We see that now the grid (window) matches the size of our vector object. However, it is entirely possible that the crop() operation does not perfectly resize our window. Take for example when we try this same operation but using ‘Italy’:

sf.italy <- world %>% 
  filter(name_long == "Italy")

r.italy <- rast()
values(r.italy) <- 1:ncell(r.italy)

# crop only italy area of world
r.crop_italy <- crop(r.italy, sf.italy)

# sanity check
plot(r.crop_italy)
plot(st_geometry(sf.italy), add=T, # use st_geometry to only plot geom col of sf object (sfc)
     col = alpha("gray", 0.4))








To fix this, we can manually adjust the window’s bounds, using the ext() function to adjust the extension feature of our raster object. Recall that the extension explicitly gives us the bounds of our raster object, given as: (\(min\) x, \(max\) x, \(min\) y, \(max\) y). We first should investigate our object and see what the cropped bounds are given as for reference:

# check the bounds of our current r.crop object
ext(r.crop_italy)

SpatExtent : 7, 18, 37, 47 (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)


From our map before, we can expand in each direction by one or two values (degrees, since this in WGS84 long-lat). To do that, we simply can define a new raster object with our manual extension values.

# define a new, custom crop window
r.crop_italy2 <- rast()
values(r.crop_italy2) <- 1:ncell(r.crop_italy2)
ext(r.crop_italy2) <- c(5, 20, 36, 48) # manually cropping
r.crop_italy2  # notice res drops

class       : SpatRaster 
size        : 180, 360, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
resolution  : 0.04166667, 0.06666667  (x, y)
extent      : 5, 20, 36, 48  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
coord. ref. : lon/lat WGS 84 (CRS84) (OGC:CRS84) 
source(s)   : memory
name        : lyr.1 
min value   :     1 
max value   : 64800 


We successfully have changed the bounds of our window, however notice that our resolution value now drops since our rast() function always creates a 180 \(\times\) 360 grid by default. As a result, each cell is approximately \(0.042^o \text{ wide}\times0.078^o \text{ tall}\). Essentially, even though we decreased our window size, we still maintain the total number of cells from before (64800!). If we tried plotting it without adjusting this, we would get a really sharp raster image:

values(r.crop_italy2) <- 1:ncell(r.crop_italy2)
plot(r.crop_italy2)








To set this back to our \(1\times1\) resolution (recommended), we simply can assign it back in manually using res():

res(r.crop_italy2) <- 1
r.crop_italy2

class       : SpatRaster 
size        : 12, 15, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
resolution  : 1, 1  (x, y)
extent      : 5, 20, 36, 48  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
coord. ref. : lon/lat WGS 84 (CRS84) (OGC:CRS84) 


Note that our final object now has the correct bounds and resolution; however, as a final note, it is important to recognize that we still need to assign values after these steps. Even if we assigned values at the very start of our object creation, after adjusting the resolution we need to reassign values; this is because when adjusting the resolution, we are just adjust the total number of cells in the raster. Since our resolution is increasing in value, we are decreasing the number of cells; it is less precise.

# assign vals
values(r.crop_italy2) <- 1:ncell(r.crop_italy2)
range(values(r.crop_italy2))

[1]   1 180


Note there are only 210 cells in our grid now to match our bounds 1:1. Indeed, we see from our final plotting that the cells are much more visible here; our bounds are successfully adjusted to capture all of Italy + some breathing room.

# sanity check
plot(r.crop_italy2)
plot(st_geometry(sf.italy), add=T, 
     col = alpha("gray", 0.4))








Note: if we want to adjust the CRS of our raster object, we can simply use project():

r.reprojected <- project(r.crop, "EPSG:2169")
crs(r.reprojected, describe=T)

                   name authority code       area                   extent
1 LUREF / Luxembourg TM      EPSG 2169 Luxembourg 5.73, 6.53, 49.44, 50.19

title: Class 04: Intro to Raster Data
text:
Vectorization
We might find it useful to move from a rast object to a sf object, such that we can perform vector operations between two sf objects.
For example, we can convert rast values to MULTIPOINT objects, using the as_points() function, then declaring it as a sf object using the command st_as_sf():

sf.point <- as.points(r.crop) %>% 
  st_as_sf() # convert into a simple feature object
head(sf.point, n=3)

Simple feature collection with 3 features and 1 field
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: -73.5 ymin: 4.5 xmax: -71.5 ymax: 4.5
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84 (CRS84)
  lyr.1          geometry
1 30707 POINT (-73.5 4.5)
2 30708 POINT (-72.5 4.5)
3 30709 POINT (-71.5 4.5)


Note our output is now a a simple feature object, with the associated geometry of points. Under the hood, this works by computing the centroid for every single cell, and assigning that centroid value as the associated geometry point.
More useful is converting raster objects into POLYGONS, using as.polygons()

# more useful: rasters -> polygons
sf.poly <- as.polygons(r.crop) %>% 
  st_as_sf()
head(sf.poly, n=3)

Simple feature collection with 3 features and 1 field
Geometry type: POLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: -74 ymin: 4 xmax: -71 ymax: 5
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84 (CRS84)
  lyr.1                       geometry
1 30707 POLYGON ((-74 5, -74 4, -73...
2 30708 POLYGON ((-73 5, -73 4, -72...
3 30709 POLYGON ((-72 5, -72 4, -71...


Plotting this newly created simple feature object onto the raster object it was generated from, we can see the resulting grid:

plot(r.crop)
plot(st_geometry(sf.poly), add=T)








We can use this to create outlines of vector objects of interest; for example, continuing with our example from before, we can can use st_filter() to get a \(1\times1\) grid covering Italy.

sf.poly_grid <- as.polygons(r.crop_italy2) %>% 
  st_as_sf() 
sf.italy_grid <- st_filter(sf.poly_grid, sf.italy, .predicate = st_intersects) # st_intersects
plot(r.crop_italy2)
plot(sf.italy_grid, add=T, col = NA, lwd = 2) 








Layering on our Italy grid, we can see the final result:

# now we can plot: cropped raster, italy, and grid overlaying italy
plot(r.crop_italy2)
plot(st_geometry(sf.italy), add=T, 
     col = alpha("salmon", 0.5), lwd=2)
plot(st_geometry(sf.italy_grid), add=T, col=alpha("gray", 0.25), lwd=1.5)








Note that we add the argument st_geometry() around the simple feature object, simply to ensure we are only plotting from the geometry column (otherwise you get annoying warning messages).
Further, note that we use st_filter(..., .predicate = st_intersects); if we want to clip all of the grids at the borders of Italy, we should use instead st_intersection(). Be careful with st_intersection() on large datasets, as it is computationally much heavier than a simple filter since it has to calculate new vertices for every clipped polygon

test <- st_intersection(sf.poly_grid, sf.italy) # cuts off all pts of the grids that dont intersect
plot(r.crop_italy2)
plot(st_geometry(test), add=T)

# Empty Vietnam Map, sanity check

Note that the DIVA data matches our Vietnam map CRS, both using WGS 84. Hence, we do not need to worry about homogenizing our projection types.




# Check for available road types in data
roads %>%
